description: I’m Lysha Rashid, a high school senior interested in aerospace engineering and web development. For this solo project, I’m building SkyShift, a website that lets visitors flip between NASA SPHEREx images of the same patch of sky taken on different dates and see what changed.
summary:
I developed EpochBlink, an interactive web tool that lets users spot moving objects by comparing infrared images of the same patch of sky taken by NASA’s SPHEREx telescope. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, I aligned two observations on a shared sky grid so users can flip between them, compare them side by side, or view a difference image that highlights changes in brightness.

The demo uses two real observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS taken about 94 minutes apart. Users can look for the comet’s motion themselves, then reveal its predicted position in each image to check what they found. Using a known comet shows how the same technique can help flag moving-object candidates for follow-up. EpochBlink makes that process accessible to students and the public, giving them a hands-on way to explore real NASA data and see how astronomers search for faint objects in the outer solar system.
details:
I built EpochBlink as a solo project for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It’s a browser-based tool that helps users spot moving objects in repeat infrared observations. I built the viewer with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and used a Python script to align image cutouts. The script uses the sky coordinates stored in the original FITS files to place both observations on the same north-up grid, so users can compare the same locations in each image.

The demo uses two calibrated SPHEREx observations from NASA’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), taken about 94 minutes apart on December 14, 2025. Users can switch rapidly between the images to make motion easier to see, compare them side by side, or use a color-coded difference view to see where brightness changed. I designed the viewer so users can look for a moving object on their own before revealing the predicted positions of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. Those positions are about 4.6 arcminutes apart, giving users a concrete way to check what they spotted.

A major design consideration was that image changes can come from noise, slight misalignment, differences in wavelength, or detector artifacts. A potential moving object would need follow-up, such as checking additional observations for consistent motion and comparing its position with known objects. By starting with a known comet, EpochBlink gives students and citizen scientists a hands-on way to practice that first step of the search using real NASA data. The same approach can help users identify candidates worth investigating in searches for distant solar system objects.
